utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, to the technical booth, the interpreters; good morning, legal officers, the registrar, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey; good morning, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic, and General Krstic. Good morning, Mr. Butler. We're going to continue with your testimony, and it is Mr. Petrusic's turn to continue. Your witness, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my learned friends from the Prosecution; good morning, Mr. Butler. The Defence wishes a good morning to all others present here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you have any evidence that the forward command post of the Drina Corps was located in the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade on the 12th, 13th, and 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there is one specific reference in one of the previous exhibits tendered, and again the specific exhibit number escapes me, where the specific identification "IKM Drina Corps" and "Bratunac" are used in the same context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was Pribicevac a forward command post during the operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As established, the location of Pribicevac was first a command post for the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Infantry Brigade, Light Infantry Brigade. It was also a command post for a group or Tactical Group that oversaw or monitored the operations of Srebrenica for two years prior. It later became the forward command post of the entire Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade as part of the operations for Krivaja-95, and into that same command post function, a good number of Drina Corps officers fell in, so it became a forward command post for the Drina Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The command post or the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, we would be talking about the forward command post at Pribicevac, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence to show who represented the Corps Commander at the command post in Vlasenica on the 14th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working under the premise that General Major Krstic was the Corps Commander on that day and that he may well have been in Zepa, with the understanding that at that time Colonel Svetozar Andric, who was assuming the position as Chief of Staff at the time, was also reportedly in Zepa, the next logical individual who would have assumed that function would have been the Chief of Operations for the Drina Corps. Now, my understanding in this regard is that the Chief of Operations of the Drina Corps was also in and around the Zepa area as well. So specifically, while I can't give you the name of an individual, the other individuals in question would have been other officers of the Drina Corps staff. The most probable one, and there would have been two that come to mind rather quickly, one would be Colonel Cerovic, the Assistant Commander for Morale, Legal, and Religious Affairs of the Drina Corps, and Colonel Popovic, the Assistant Commander for Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Regarding the change of the Corps Commander, were the brigade commanders or the brigades informed of that change? Because as you say, this change took place on the 13th. Were they informed on that same day of this change?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the previous -- as at least one previous exhibit has demonstrated, the response by the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade to a Drina Corps order that we do not possess, in reading that response, I conclude that that case specifically, the Bratunac Brigade, was informed of a change of command, and my presumption is that based on that document, that the other brigades would have been informed as well. However, that again -- that information would have been available to them by the late evening of the 13th or the early morning of the 14th hours, so I can't specifically say the brigade commanders would have been aware of that change of command on 13 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the written documents of the other brigades, the Zvornik, the Milici, the Vlasenica, and Birca Brigades, as well as the Rogatica Brigade, among those documents is there any evidence to show that the Commanders were informed of the change at the head of the corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I previously indicated, of the units that you've listed, the written documents that I have reflect only Bratunac Brigade and Zvornik Brigade. I do not possess the material documents for the other units that you've listed. So I cannot answer that. I can only say that in the case of the Bratunac Brigade, I have a piece of information that indicates that there was a change of command notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that piece of information from the Bratunac Brigade, is a date indicated when the change took place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. The specific phrase, and again it comes out rather awkward in English, is "hitherto," which, being American and not English, I had to ask -- do some research on what exactly that meant, "hitherto" reflecting from that point and prior. So my conclusion is that that change of command or that date is reflective of their notification on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher for his assistance to find Exhibit 556, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In its questions, the Defence will proceed from the assumption that this piece of information is an authentic document, although that has been disputed because this is an intercepted telephone conversation conducted on the 14th of July, 1995, at 20.38 between Major Jokic and Major General Zivanovic who is at Zlatar. In the third line of this conversation, General Zivanovic says to Major Jokic, "Take this as an order." Mr. Butler, somebody who has been replaced and relieved of his duty as commander, can he issue orders to an immediate subordinate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reviewing the intercepts within the context and with specifically this intercept, because this issue and this specific intercept flies counter to the theory that we've examined, one of the things that I have done in looking at this is trying to come to grips with under what circumstances and why that phrase specifically is there. One of the possible reasons that I would have, and in many regards this is supported by the other information pertaining to the lack of communications with General Krstic and, in fact, in many case supported by statements that have come out of the interview, that there was also a discussion between Colonel Obrenovic, or Major Obrenovic at the time, and General Krstic related to the same topical area. So in this regards, and as I believe I've noted in direct, the top line, the frequency, was not active, again potentially implying a communications difficulty. But in putting this all together, what I believe we have in this case is General Zivanovic still as a superior officer in the VRS, in fact giving an order to the duty officer Major Jokic and indicating to him that he should take this as an order, the presumption being that he, General Zivanovic, is authorised, particularly in this case, to give that order. Moving back off that, the question then becomes by what authorisation General Zivanovic is giving this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In this same conversation a few lines down, General Zivanovic indicates in tactical terms, I would say, what Major Jokic needs to do -- or rather, the unit of the Zvornik Brigade, when he says, "Then it means good weapons, good reconnaissance and taking good action against all of that." And then towards the very end of the conversation he says again, "Therefore blockade, blockade. The units will be there by dawn." Mr. Butler, is he, that is General Zivanovic, indicating how units should be deployed in the sense of a command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific intercept, what I believe he's doing -- he's not specifically indicating how units would be deployed as a command. What he's doing is indicating in broad terms the type of broad actions that he wants the duty officer to pass to Obrenovic what he should be doing during the course of the evening, for the first part; and for the second part, indicating that block it, do the best that you can, and be aware that reinforcement and other units will be there by dawn, dawn in this case being the morning of the 15th. And as we know from the further information, the units of the Zvornik Brigade withdrawing from Zepa arrive the morning of the 15th back in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The time of this conversation is the 14th of July, 1995, at 2020 hours. That is what the Defence wishes to note. The next exhibit is 558. The date is the 14th of July, 1995, and the conversation at 2056 hours between a major and General Zivanovic - X. Mr. Butler, in the seventh line of this intercept, the Major addresses the General and says, "How can I find out --" he's addressing "X" and asking him, "How can I find out where General Zivanovic is as I've been waiting here for him on his orders since 1700 hours." Does that mean that someone is continuing to act on General Zivanovic's orders and to carry out his orders, or rather, that Major General Zivanovic is still issuing orders to his -- to subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly your first explanation is probably the most technically accurate one considering the identification of "M," the major, is unidentified. So not knowing how "M" the major is, it's difficult to make the next leap, but clearly that individual is waiting for General Zivanovic on his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So in this case too, we have an order which was passed on to somebody from General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure it qualifies as an order. It's a statement that a Major has been waiting for General Zivanovic at a location on his order. I don't know if that qualifies as a passing on of an order in a formal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But in this intercept, in this case, reference is made to an order among the participants.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference made to the order is the individual Major was told by General Zivanovic to be here waiting for him. In the scheme of orders and instructions in commands, in my mind, looking at that, it's less a formalised, "I'm giving you a series of formal instructions," rather than a general is a superior officer telling a major, unidentified, "Be there at this time and wait for me." It's tough to tell what the context is, but I wouldn't read too much into it on one line, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may the Defence be allowed to read the entire intercept? It is not long. So: "X: Just a moment, to Colonel Vukovic. M: How it's going? X: We're fine, how about you? M: How can I find out where General Zivanovic is? I've been waiting here for him on his orders since 1700 hours. X: He's here. M: What? X: He's here. M: There? X: Yes. M: Put me through to him. X: I'll try to now. Z: Good evening, Vuko. M: Things are all right, good, here. I did everything in the spirit of what I received last night. And this morning /?he/ called me Natasku? /word unknown/ and I came here this morning at around 10 o'cock and I /as written/. Z: Major! M: Yes, yes, I understand you. Z: I have just come from the checkpoint ... M: Could you repeat that, please? Z: I said that paper which was sent - there is one - from Blagojevic, about me. M: Okay. Z: Read my conclusions. M: I understand. Z: Because (from here on drowned out by previously recorded conversation) M: Yes, sir. I understand, completely, and then we'll focus on the one down there. (drowned out by previously recorded conversation) M: I understand. I'm going to my post up there. Z: Listen. Where are your boys there? M: Well, my boys are now in the western part, working there as of today. Everything's in place. Sweet as a nut. Z: Excellent. M: I did that today. Z: ... (mumbles something briefly) M: Yes, sir. Z: Take care. M: Take care."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From this entire conversation, Mr. Butler, it is clear that the Major, as a participant, and Zivanovic as the other participant, are discussing a certain military situation, and in a part of that conversation, Ivanovic is cautioning the Major and telling him to read the conclusions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a correct phrase, sir, read my conclusions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the Major is telling General Zivanovic where his forces are distributed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And does General Zivanovic express his approval of that distribution of forces when he says "excellent"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher for his assistance, and Exhibit number 532, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska issued by Lieutenant-Colonel Milan Gvero. The date is unclear, illegible, but it is July 1995. In view of the format of this order and the units to which it is addressed, the question is: The units to whom this order was issued, are obliged to inform the Main Staff on the execution of this order?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With this specific order and coupling that with the follow-on order for the Drina Corps, which essentially repeats this and redistributes it to the brigades, I would not interpret it as the brigades are responsible for informing the Main Staff specifically. The order, as written, indicates -- I believe the phrase that they use is -- okay. In this case they do not use the phrase, so let me -- in this specific one they talk about the Republika Srpska Main Staff. So in this case, I don't believe they use the generic phrase "superior command." Again looking at this, I read there along the lines of the Drina Corps, as the primary command, having to inform the Main Staff through interim reports. I do not read this, and I do not believe it is intended that the subordinate brigades are to inform the Main Staff directly through the use of interim reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It is undisputed that the Main Staff has issued an order to lower-level units, in this case, brigades, is it not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case the Main Staff has issued an order to the Drina Corps commands, the IKMs, and several of the Drina Corps brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, can I have Exhibit 649, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: An order of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, dated the 17th of July, 1995, signed by the Commander, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic. The appointment of commanders of the mentioned orders, and that is Lieutenant-Colonel Kesarevic, does that imply that Lieutenant-Colonel Kesarevic is obliged, after carrying out activities envisaged by this order, to inform the Main Staff through regular and interim reports to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska or to -- that is, to its Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance, the document specifies that the deadline for the completion of the task by a designated date and an order for further engagement towards Cerska shall be imposed, meaning that Colonel Kesarevic -- I hope I pronounced that correctly -- should propose a future operations plan to me, again in this case it would be General Mladic, by July 19, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit number 364/2, please, Mr. Usher. The tab 17th of July, tab 14/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the Defence will once again ask the following questions under the presumption of authenticity of this document. This is an intercepted conversation. It was -- it took place on the 17th of July at 2030 hours. Participants are Krstic and "X." In this conversation, Krstic asks "X," "With whose approval did you send soldiers down there?" and "X" answers, "On orders from the Main Staff." Does that mean that the Main Staff having issued the order, in this case to "X," the Commander of this unit, bypassed the chain of command through the Corps Commander or the Deputy Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I read the whole thing before I give you my answer. I don't want to answer it out of context, here. My answer to that, and I just wanted to confirm this because I've gone over this one before as part of my analysis, is that it only -- your conclusion makes sense if you're willing to assume that "X" and the unit of "X" are under the command of the Drina Corps. That presumption is not indicative in the order, for example. "X" could be the commander of a Main Staff unit or another unit which General Krstic may have thought he had some right to command or had some string on their resources. So without knowing again who "X" is and what the function and purpose of "X" is prior, I can't presume that "X" is in fact a subordinate of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, "X" mentions Potocari, and that's the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "X" says he was up in Potocari; he had to check it out. All "X" is doing is giving a physical location on the ground where he was at a point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, "X" says, "I have just come recently from my area of responsibility just to make your acquaintance," and he talks about Potocari. So is Potocari in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, Potocari is in the zone of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, are there cases and is it possible for a superior command, in this case the Main Staff, to take over the command over subordinate units, Drina Corps that is, in the whole area of responsibility of the Drina Corps or in a limited area thereof?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand what you're asking, sir, what you're asking is, is a series of two theoreticals. Theoretical number one, is it possible for a Superior Command to take over, and if I read the transcript correctly, over the command over subordinate units, the whole area of responsibility in one sense; and then the next one is the theoretical, is it possible for them to take over command of a limited small unit. Going back to the 7 [sic] July 1995 order, the previous exhibit, 649, I believe that's an excellent example of how the Main Staff can take over limited command of select assets, some including the Drina Corps, for a specific period. Going back to your first one, whether or not it's possible for them to come in and essentially take over whole commands, brigade-size formations, if you will, I don't see practical applications of that, and I don't see evidence that supports that in my research, unless we're physically talking about the resubordination of brigades from one command to another command for battlefield reasons on the ground. One would think that with the work load of the Main Staff over -- having to oversee the activities of six corps, that that would be a bit much for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there seems to be a mistake in the transcript. Instead of the 7th of July, it should read 17th of July since Mr. Butler in his response referred to document -- to Exhibit 649.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in your expert opinion, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you stated that General Mladic supervised the operation and the events related and everything, in fact, related to the Krivaja-95 operation. If it is indeed the case, did General Mladic have an obligation to let the meeting in Potocari on the 11th and on the 12th of July, the last one being in the morning hours, to let his Corps Commander lead the meeting or perhaps his deputy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic is clearly the Commander of the Main Staff and, in effect, the senior ranking and Commander of the army who answers only to the President of the republic. Understanding the context of this meeting, the fact that General Mladic, whether he wanted to designate or not delegate the details of it to his Chief of Staff or to a Corps Commander or to anyone else, is his decision. And clearly when one looks at the style of General Mladic, certainly as envisioned by -- or certainly as demonstrated by the video evidence that has been seen to date relative to Srebrenica, he very much is hands-on and involved with certainly the public aspects of these events, and these meetings certainly qualify as public aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can we count these meetings that fall under the heading of "command of subordinate officers"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, sir? I'm not sure what regard "command of subordinate officers." I mean, clearly he's giving instructions to his officers, he's giving instructions to the Dutch UN representatives that are present, and he's giving instructions to the Muslim civilian representatives who are present. So it's an exercise of General Mladic giving instructions to everybody concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the last part of our cross-examinations, we would like to go over into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's go into private session, please, for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are in open session now. Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Since we left at the meetings, let me just briefly ask you, the meetings on the 11th and the 12th had -- General Krstic was there, General Mladic was there, other high-ranking officers of the corps were there. Can we -- can you assume that there were other meetings related to military matters, aside from the meetings that we see on the video, between the VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- my understanding is that there would be other meetings, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From a military sense, when could you expect the VRS command structure that was present in the area of Potocari and Bratunac on the 10th, 11th, and 12th, when could you expect for them to have knowledge that there were a fair number of Muslim men gathered and a large group of individuals in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look back at the military situation and where the units were laid out, and as previously noted, the VRS positions were in the hills, not only along the route and -- or along surrounding Srebrenica town and later on the 11th in the town but certainly in a position to overlook the road from Srebrenica to Potocari and then Potocari itself, the presumption is that they would have been able to observe the movement of the civilian population from Srebrenica to Potocari on the late afternoon, early evening hours of the 11th. And certainly either during the evening hours of the 11th or certainly by first light on the 12th, been in a position to physically observe the composition of the large number of people at Potocari. Certainly they may not have been able to pull out numbers and everything else, but as the witness statements and Dutch testimony indicates, the sheer number of people around that area, it should not have been difficult for reconnaissance units or individuals conducting personal reconnaissance to get a broad idea as to general numbers or general percentage of men, women, and children as part of the larger crowds. So fixing a date of time, it could have occurred as early as the evening hours of 11 July, sir, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, given that the transcripts of those meetings, what we know of them, obviously they're not complete transcripts, show that on the 11th, General Mladic is interested in the Muslim soldiers. When is the first time that we see from the transcripts that General Mladic actually makes reference to males between the ages of 16 and 60, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, at the third meeting that occurs at 1000 hours on 12 July 1995, General Mladic makes that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again, if you can recall, when approximately did Muslim people in Potocari start to get put on buses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In reading and in reviewing the testimony of the Dutch and other survivors, by the mid-afternoon, almost -- and I can't really qualify it in a period of time when the first buses leave for Kladanj, there are also a series of buses that depart that are filled with men that are going to Bratunac. So again, that process occurred in the mid-afternoon hours of 12 July, and we see the men being put on buses and taken to Bratunac at approximately the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So given that time frame that you've discussed, from the evening of July 11th when the VRS could have first found out about men in Potocari and the afternoon of July 12th when men had their IDs taken and were put on buses, who was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps at that time and present at those locations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been General Major Krstic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as the Chief of Staff, as you've described earlier, would one of his principal responsibilities be the planning and organising of military operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is his primary job function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did the VRS first become aware of large numbers of Muslim men from the column and that they would have the opportunity to -- sorry. Let me start over and phrase that a little better. When was it -- did it become clear to the VRS that they were able to capture or they would be able to capture large numbers of Muslim men from the column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intercepts, as we have them, indicate that by approximately 0300 hours on the morning of 12 July, the Muslim [sic] lower commanders on the ground or along the road were becoming aware of the existence of a column. That column formed during the day and continued to move through 12 July. The presumption would be that sometime certainly by the afternoon of 12 July or early evening hours at the latest, they would have been capturing Muslim men from the column. As to when an exact awareness of when that would have been, I can't answer that specifically, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Butler. You said at the beginning of your answer "the Muslim lower commanders on the ground."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. That should be the VRS lower commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before the evening hours of July 13th, were many, many hundreds of Muslims in fact captured along the Bratunac-Milici road and shipped off to various places that you've discussed before, Bratunac, Kravica warehouse, those places?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again at that time period, General Krstic was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and would have been involved primarily in planning -- well, excuse me, not primarily but certainly would have been involved in planning operations if he was doing his job as defined by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, counsel brought up, in the cross-examination, a conclusion you made in your report regarding the leadership role of General Krstic in the attack of Srebrenica. Now, I've asked you to assemble some of the documents that are actually in support of that theory of yours. Could you just take us through them very briefly. I know you've already spoken of them, so I don't think we need to spend much time, but I do -- I would like it if you would remind the Court of what -- the real meaning of that paragraph. What backed up that paragraph in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, that series of documents which are now exhibits which demonstrate the situation that certainly General Zivanovic, the Corps Commander, is not physically present and that General Krstic, the Chief of Staff, is present at the forward command post and running that operation. I would refer to Exhibit 431, and again, I won't discuss it in detail, which indicates discussion between the two of them, and this date is 8 July. I would reference Exhibit 432, which is a 9 July report to the Drina Corps IKM, again, directed personally for General Krstic at that location. I would note Exhibit 433, which is the excerpt of the Bratunac Brigade daily combat report for 10 July 1995, noting for the first time the physical presence of General Mladic and General-Major Zivanovic, as well as the presence of General-Major Krstic in the zone of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade and of course, the forward command post at Pribicevac falls in that zone. Exhibit 435 intercepted radio telephone communication between General Krstic and Lieutenant Colonel Krsmanovic who is the Chief of Transportation Services for the Drina Corps with regard to the assembly of buses. Exhibit 508, again, a discussion by the duty officer at Badem, 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, and a subscriber at Zlatar, the Drina Corps, and while we don't know who the correspondents are other than the broad duty officer identification is "X," that duty officer indicates the physical presence of General Krstic "here." The presumption here is that the duty officer is in the operations centre at the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade at this time. Exhibit 539, another "X" and "Y" intercept, last line noting the request of fuel being forwarded to Krstic, and noting that so far 50 buses have been obtained. Exhibit 364, again, a conversation between General Krstic and a certain Ognjenovic, whom I believe to be Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic, a member of the Drina Corps operations staff at this time; and then further, a conversation between him and Krsmanovic again, and as previously noted, Colonel Krsmanovic, the Chief of Transportation. And looking at both parts of the conversation, it's clear that the specific area that we're talking about is in the area of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade within the tactical situation, and the second part pertaining to movement of buses. Exhibit 440, again, a synopsis of a conversation between the two correspondents, Krstic wants the buses to start moving immediately. Exhibit 446, another discussion, and again the principle players here, General Krstic, Colonel Kosoric, the Chief of Intelligence of the Drina Corps, a notation up front noting that Krsmanovic, the Chief of Transportation, set off towards Krstic's location 15 minutes ago, and Sobot, in this case another officer of the rear services branch of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you note the times as you're going through these so we can see the time, how they're related in time sequence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. This one is 1305, and I believe the date inclusive that we've been discussing is all 12 July, sir. 1345 hours, and this is Exhibit 509, and the back end of the conversation, again, an acknowledgment, "I can put you up there to General Krstic. He's in charge of this attack." Again, an awareness on the part of the subscriber "O," a duty officer, and as we've discussed earlier in my testimony as to the roles and functions of the duty officer, the individual who, on behalf of the Commander, is the focal point of the gathering of all of the information that's coming in. So presumably the duty officer is in a position to be aware of the events that are occurring and the context in which they're occurring. Exhibit 510, and I'll just go to the relevant part here, time is 1440, the back end of the conversation in a series of conversations, and the way we've already discussed the exhibit, but again, Krstic coming on the line asking to be put through to Colonel Krsmanovic. The last line, "Come on, put me through to him again, Zlatar," an implication -- or an inference that he's calling to the Zlatar switch, and he's angry at them because he dropped off the line. Exhibit 529, this one 13 July 1995, time of 2040, conversation between Krstic, General Krstic, and Borovcanin who, as discussed earlier, is Lieutenant Colonel Ljubisa Borovcanin, who is in charge of the MUP Special Police Unit that is operating along the road, Bratunac-Konjevic Polje, with the Drina Corps. Exhibit -- I believe that covers the series of exhibits. I don't want to go too fast. I believe that covers the series of exhibits. The last one, 483, the base exhibit pertaining to the Zepa operations order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's signed as Chief of Staff, General Krstic as Chief of Staff on the 13th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. That is signed by General Krstic as the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then I think the last two exhibits are just General Mladic's and President Karadzic's statements regarding the leadership role of General Krstic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Exhibit 99, as we've discussed previously, and Exhibit 482, also discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Mladic's statements were very specific regarding the Srebrenica and Zepa attacks. He describes the leadership of General Krstic as Chief of Staff or Corps Commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, thank you. And just to clarify the record, one -- I think Mr. Butler identified an Exhibit as 539, and Ms. Keith tells me it should be 359. At this point we may be getting a little dyslexic, all of us, so we'll ... Now, Mr. Butler, 14 July, that was the day the records indicate the attack on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- according to the operations plan and the other information we have, the beginning of the attack on Zepa occurred early morning hours of 14 July, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any intercepts that have General Krstic on them on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As previously noted, we have no intercepts of General Krstic on 14 July 1995 that reflect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: However, there are indications in the investigation and in the records that Major Obrenovic had discussions with General Krstic on the 14th of July regarding the situation up in Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the 15th, 16th, 17th, are there intercepts with General Krstic on those dates?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are I believe at least one, perhaps two on the 15th, and numerous ones on the 16th and 17th, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are those generally consistent with a Corps Commander checking in or monitoring the situation in his zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want to briefly go back to an exhibit the Defence discussed, the Main Staff order signed by General Gvero on 13 July, Exhibit 532/A, and there was a suggestion that or a question to you whether or not this order would have required the brigades to report back to the Main Staff. You made reference to a Drina Corps order that was directly related to that Main Staff order, and I have that now, and if I could ask you to take a look at it. It's Exhibit 462/A, and is that specific as to the reporting responsibilities of the brigades?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order, and as I've discussed previously, is almost a verbatim copy of the General Gvero order. If you go to the final paragraph 8 on page 3 of the English translation, it notes, "Through interim reports, ensure all units are kept informed of the current situation in areas of responsibility so that the Command of the Drina Corps may be able to take measures in good time." I believe this very clearly articulates that the reports are to go to the Command of the Drina Corps so they can take measures in good time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could get the exhibit that shows the quote from the 15 July interim combat report, I think it may be 29 right there. I don't think we'll use the exhibit. Mr. Butler, you have read this enough times. Could you tell us -- again I'll make reference to the part -- sorry, it's 610, but that's all right, I'll just make reference to it. The part I'm referring to of the interim combat report is the part where Colonel Pandurevic says something to the effect that, "The additional burden for us are the large number of Muslims located in schools throughout the area of the responsibility of the brigade, as well as obligations of security and restoration of terrain. The Command cannot take care of these problems any longer as it has neither the material nor the resources. If no one takes care of this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." Now, we've gone through your interpretation of that somewhat cryptic communication regarding dealing with the Muslim prisoners throughout the schools. Would this be difficult to understand by itself if the receiver of it did not understand the context by which it was being said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that that's a, that's a fair assumption. If you did not understand the context of what was going on, this would be pretty meaningless to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when was this sent to the Corps Command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual report, the outgoing time stamp reflects, I believe, either 18 or 2000 hours on 15 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is there any information in the record that would indicate whether or not the Corps Commander, General Krstic, did in fact have knowledge of the murder operation that was going on in the Zvornik Brigade on 15 July and prior to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would in that event refer back to the series of exhibits which reflect the conversation which occurred between General-Major Krstic and Colonel Beara with regards to the "packages" and having no effective way to deal with them. As I've noted as that conversation as well, certainly from reading that conversation, because it's noted by one of the subscribers, and I don't know whether it's Colonel Beara or General Krstic off the top of my head, that the "line is open and we shouldn't discuss it in that manner," they're clearly attempting to talk around the meat of the subject. Again, another clear indication that in trying to talk around what the real part of the subject is, both correspondents are fully aware of what the context of the conversation is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for one or two last questions, Your Honour, could we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let us go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now. I think this is a good time to have a break. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I see on the transcript it says "private session," but Mr. McCloskey said "closed session." Just for clarification for the court reporters, because they always ask me, do you want it private, closed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the difference, but I want it as closed as we can get it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have a half-hour break now, and after that, we'll come back for the questions of the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I think you have something to communicate to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In the break that we just had, General Krstic had certain health problems linked to his amputated leg, and as soon as that was noted, the doctor on duty found that an urgent medical treatment was required to deal with the injury, so that General Krstic is now being treated. However, we have conferred with him, and he agrees that we continue with the proceedings in his absence, and he has given a written statement to that effect, which has been provided to the registrar. The statement is in the Serbian language, but if I may translate it, it says that General Krstic agrees that we continue the hearings in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have no objection to proceeding in the absence of General Krstic, in light of the fact that he has filed a written waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement is indeed in B/C/S, but we trust Mr. Petrusic because, unfortunately, we do not understand the B/C/S. What will be the number of this document, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the General's statement will be marked and admitted into evidence as 714, Exhibit 714. Fine. So we can resume our proceedings, and it is now the turn of us Judges to put questions to the witness, Mr. Richard Butler, and I give the floor, therefore, to Judge Fouad Riad. Excuse me. I beg your pardon. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours, but I see that Exhibit 714 is in the series of the Prosecutor's exhibits, and I don't think this should be a Prosecutor's exhibit. I draw that to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry. My mistake. I'll get the proper number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon, for drawing our attention to this. I myself was surprised that the Defence had produced all those documents prior to this one, 713, therefore. So what will be the number now, Madam Registrar? Or we can deal with the matter at the end of the session. So let me give the floor now to Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I've been listening carefully to your very comprehensive testimony. I've learned a lot from it. I would invite you to shed some more light, to help me understand as somebody who is not military. Some of my questions I don't think need closed session, but if there is any suspicion, we can immediately close the session. You mentioned a statement -- I think you mentioned a statement by President Karadzic at the time, stating that General Krstic -- he was not a General perhaps at that time -- "Krstic planned the operation in front of me and I approved that task for Srebrenica, which he did exceptionally well." I quoted you as much as I can. Then you said, "I corroborate that statement." Now, what do you corroborate in that statement? In other words, what is the planning of the operation? What does this entail or include, military or civilian, the fighting, or the execution? Could you tell it to me without being too sophisticated militarily?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In doing my analysis and looking at the outside material, the open-source press, in which case this would fall under, what I indicate when I corroborate it is that it in fact is a corroboration by President Karadzic of, at a minimum, the military planning aspects of the operation. Now, as to whether he physically planned it in front of him or an awareness of the president of the planning process, I don't know, but -- and again, keeping with the more limited or more conservative views that I have pertaining to what qualifies as criminal and what qualifies as military, and if I'm not sure I will default to the military one, I would only note that my judgement is that that particular statement corroborates the military planning aspect. I wouldn't take it further than that without additional information, which I don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would the military aspect include the transportation of the men to the camps, for instance, and keeping them in the camps as one step?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military -- certainly that is a military function, sir. Where the problem that I would have is trying to, again, get in the head of President Karadzic and try to determine whether or not he is only referring to the Krivaja-95 operations plan, which it would be a natural assumption to make that as the president of the Supreme Command, he would see that plan and certainly be briefed on it; or whether it's taking it to the next step, which is the planning and execution process of moving the men up to execution sites and things of that nature. So I'm unable to make a determination based on that individual piece of information as to what part of the planning process President Karadzic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So the Krivaja plan did not include transportation or anything except fighting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krivaja plan as written does -- only indicates that prisoners will be assembled and dealt with as part of the normal function of a corps military operation. The Krivaja plan as written does not go into the next series of steps as part of criminal act, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As written, but who is supposed to execute it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard, and as I've discussed as part of the testimony, as the military portion of the operation and then the criminal portion of the operation which is conducted by the military takes off, General Krstic as the Chief of Staff would be the person who would by position and, certainly as the facts suggest, by knowledge be an integral part of that process, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, there was also a mention that Mr. Karadzic would -- considered General Krstic a very prominent general, and even he could compete with Mladic. Do you think that still General Mladic would be able to pass over Krstic and, let us say, dominate the situation and do the whole thing, or would this be contrary to your findings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the things that needs to be understood about that particular excerpt is, and one of the reasons why I don't put that much validity in except a very limited manner, is the fact that that excerpt was part of a larger speech by General -- or by President Karadzic on 4 August 1995 where he, in effect, removed General Mladic from the chief -- as the Chief and Commander of the army, the Commander of the Main Staff, and tried to move him sideways, so to speak, and appoint himself the Commander of the army and move General Mladic into a position as his advisor, in effect, taking him out of a position of codified command and removing him to an advisory position. Understanding that that's the context of the entire thrust of the conversation, it's not unreasonable to assume that he's going to certainly try and downplay the role of General Mladic and up-play the role of General Krstic. In fact, if you go back and look at the 4 August 1995 daily combat report for the Bratunac Brigade, that daily combat report reflects that on 4 August in the afternoon or during the day, President Karadzic in fact did travel to Srebrenica and meet with and do a walk-through tour with General Krstic. Knowing several hours later that President Karadzic in fact tried to remove General Mladic as the Commander of the Main Staff, certainly you could infer that part of the conversation that they were having on that day would have been a discussion relative to whether or not General Krstic would publicly support the president of the republic in that move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, would this -- where would the, what can I say, the withdrawal of General Zivanovic fit in this case? Why did Zivanovic, why was he removed in that period, if you know about it, and replaced by Krstic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, sir, is the million-dollar question, and I really don't have a solid answer. We understand from both public statements, and we also understand from the interview that he gave to a correspondent a year after the events occurred, that he was suffering health problems. And if you would refer back to the video exhibit where it shows the walk-through on 11 July 1995 in company with General Mladic and General Krstic, one of the statements attributed to General Zivanovic, and if I believe the quote is correct, he says, "My blood pressure must now be 600 over 300." Again, I don't have a background in medicine, but clearly the implication is that, you know, perhaps high blood pressure. We have in the statements of Drazan Erdemovic, he makes a specific reference to information that he understands relative to information he gained as part of that walk-through, his impression that General Zivanovic was leaving as part of a planned event, that it was not a spontaneous act, meaning that Mr. Erdemovic felt that his view was this is not a spontaneous removal, that General Zivanovic seemed to indicate that he knew his time was coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You added yourself that, I don't find the quotation exactly, but it was a very -- it was not the most propitious period for a transition of command.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one looks at the operations in a strictly military sense, that Krivaja-95 as an operation militarily alone ends at a fixed point in time and then subsequent to that Stupcanica-95, the operation for the takedown of the Zepa enclave occurs in sequence afterwards, you could make the argument that it would be a logical time to replace the Commander, particularly if it was understood that the Commander is going to be replaced by the Chief of Staff, and you would have absolutely no loss in the knowledge base and the visions of what the operations were supposed to be. Overlaying the context of the military events as they occurred, which shows that it wasn't a clean break and, in fact, the unexpected breakthrough by the 28th Infantry Division or the unexpected movement of the column out clouds that issue. You don't get a clean break. And when you look at it from that aspect, it wouldn't seem to be a good time to do that. The only other inference that I can make that adds another fact to that but doesn't, unfortunately, clear it up, is the fact that General Zivanovic, after the fact, goes to great pains to make it known, on a public level, that he was out of there as early as midnight on the 11th of July. He didn't want to be associated with anything after the midnight of the 11th of July. So again, a series of facts, and I'm not exactly sure what that means with respect to the intent to replace one General with another General. So that sense it remains ambiguous for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the bottom line would be that in the eyes of the president, the Supreme Commander, Krstic was the man fit for the job.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably he may not have appointed him unless he felt that he did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And with the support of the president?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as the president is the only person who can formally appoint him as the commander, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in the light of this, how much do you think he could be unrelated to the events? For instance, you mentioned the civilian authorities of Srebrenica. Could there be some kind of distribution of roles and Krstic would be just the military man and the civilian authorities would be handling, let us say, the rest, the transfer of prisoners, the executions, and so on? Is that, militarily speaking, a very logical plan, division of roles and power?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While in the abstract it might appear to be a logical break-up of responsibilities, the fact basis completely supports the fact that the military was the primary agency responsible for doing all of this, to include the fact that the military was, through the Ministry of Defence, requisitioning civilian assets and civilian resources in order to accomplish this mission. Given the state of military affairs and everything else, I don't believe it would have been realistic to believe that the military could only fight the battle. The civilian leadership could handle just the civilian aspects of moving Muslim civilians, the two would not get mixed up somewhere, and again the fact that the civilian leadership, the local civilian leadership didn't have the resources to accomplish that mission anyway. So certainly the military had primacy in this role, and I don't believe that the civilian leadership would have thought that they could not have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, when you speak about the military function, does it -- do you speak in the light or bearing in mind the chain of command as the regular army or just the military people with weapons, doing what they like?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in this context and what I hope I've demonstrated through the fact base that has been presented, is that one of the fundamental tenets of this entire series of events is the underlying organisation and structure involved. Certainly in isolation, one can make the argument that an individual Muslim civilian in Potocari being killed or maybe a group of five or ten being killed can be an isolated event or along the road an isolated event, but when you string them altogether, particularly tracking the implied organisational process that takes the civilians from Potocari, the female and the children and the elderly from Potocari and deposits them at Kladanj under military control, and then you take the implied organisational things that have to have happened to first collect the Muslim men in Bratunac, bring the additional Muslim men who were captured from the column to holding sites at Bratunac, organise their movement into the zone of another brigade, the Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and then the systematic executions in series and how the specialised equipment needed to bury the dead moves from site to site, when you look at that in its entire context and then overlay on top of that how a corps command and staff would have controlled that given their roles, responsibilities, and functions, then the individual facts that all lock that into place through the series, and because of that whole series of events and how I look at that, understanding the military structure and how it would have worked by a military, it would be impossible to conclude that these are a series of random widespread individual events of which that there was no or extremely limited control over, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, in light of this orderly chain of command, you mentioned that General Krstic gave orders that women and children should not be molested, shall not be hurt, and he was obeyed, except one who was abused. I noted that down. Did he only concentrate on women and children and mention nothing according -- you don't say the people should not be -- the civilians should not be touched or he said women and children? And what do you infer from that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He makes two specific comments. The one, the first comment you refer to was from an intercepted communication where he's discussing the issue with a subordinate Drina Corps officer. The second is a public statement that he makes in Potocari compound on 12 July 1995, where he notes that the operation is continuing under the Drina Corps to liberate the entire Srebrenica area, municipality presumably, and that he also makes a statement -- and I can't remember it completely so I won't quote it, so I won't misquote it -- but he also makes a statement relative to the treatment of the civilian population, something along the lines, I guess, of they'll be moved to wherever they want to go. So in that sense, he makes those two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The statement concerning the women and children you said was obeyed, except one exception. Was the other one -- had he given the same orders concerning men? Would it have been obeyed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is -- I don't have any evidence that he gave the same order concerning men, and to be honest, sir, again you're asking me to get into General Krstic's head on that one. I don't know whether if he gave that order it would be obeyed, sir. It's real speculation on my part, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. It's a twofold question. You said first he didn't give the order, I gather from the answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But the other thing: According to the chain of command, would he have been obeyed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he gave that order according to the chain of command, certainly all the troops under his command would have obeyed that order or should have obeyed that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You gave the options of a commander who disapproves of a situation, and you said -- you gave several things. You said he can protest, he can withdraw. Do you think, under the circumstances in this very specific situation, was it possible for a commander to withdraw or to show his disapproval? I don't know if that was the case of Zivanovic, but could General Krstic have done that with impunity, with impunity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you've indicated, sir, I don't know that that wasn't the case with General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What about others? Was there any other who disapproved of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer your question in two parts, sir. The first part is that I do not have any information, throughout the entirety of my analysis of the VRS, that at any given point in time a senior officer, battalion, brigade, certainly a corps commander, was at any point in time ever prevented from or operating under a climate of fear pertaining to what he approved of or did not approve of actions. I would remind the Court that in November 1994, General Galic, for again circumstances not clear, left as the Commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So in that respect, I don't have any evidence base which would suggest that officers who disobeyed or not disobeyed but disapproved of the conduct of the overall course of the war or of the orders they were following felt a compelling need to follow them for individual fear. I mean, this was not the Nazi SS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just as a footnote. You said about Zivanovic, you said he made it clear that by the 11th of July, midnight, he was not involved. Wasn't that a way of disassociating himself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, again, I wouldn't want to speculate too far into that. All I know is we have the one fact, the one public statement that he's made to that regards. We certainly are able, through the fact base, to demonstrate that he was in fact there on the 12th, and he was in fact there on the 13th, and he continued to be in the area on the 14th. So that is an inference. But based on those two, I wouldn't go that much further, personally, in trying to theorise the circumstances that General Zivanovic did that under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You're not putting him in the same category of the other General, Galic, I think?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just using General Galic as an example of the fact that corps commanders did change through the war, and I only used General Galic. I know there were other corps commanders as well, but that they did change throughout the war. And while we don't understand the reasons why all of these corps commanders changed, there's nothing in the information or the evidence base that I have that would suggest that these senior VRS officers were operating under a climate of fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: My last question, you mentioned that Colonel Pandurevic mentioned that he would not consider the -- he would not consider operation Krivaja as finished until it has -- until all the issues are dealt with in the zone of Zvornik Brigade, until all the issues are dealt with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you left this a little bit in suspense. What does he mean by "all the issues"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the content of that specific comment and based on the events that were occurring, there were only two issues occurring in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade at that time: one, the combat operations against the column, and the other, the mass executions that were occurring at the previously identified sites. As to which one is he specifically referring to, I don't know that I could take that next step, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have perhaps a question that requires a closed session, but I'll keep it. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I asked many questions as your testimony, perhaps too many from your point of view, as your testimony has proceeded; but let me tell you in advance I've got about a dozen questions so that you may, if you care to pace your answers --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a blank pad, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So that we have lots of time for Judge Rodrigues' questions as well. Several of them are, in the beginning, based upon your analysis of the roles of Chief of Staff in the VRS based, as you explained, partly on earlier JNA regulations, partly on what you saw as evidence of the way they were implemented or adjusted during this period. My first question is, would you say that the Commander could under the existing regulations and practices and might be likely to delegate more responsibility for implementations of his broader orders to the Chief of Staff than to the lower line officers? In other words, might a Commander be more likely to give broader discretion in the implementation of his overall orders to a Chief of Staff than to his lower line officers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way the system is designed, ma'am, that's exactly what is supposed to happen, the Chief of Staff taking the broader guidance, and then it becomes his function as the head of the staff to take the broad guidance and turn that into executable orders or specified taskings for the subordinate commands and commanders. That's how the system is designed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My next question is, in the specific situation we had here, if an order to the Assistant Corps Commander who was the chief of security, the assistant commander for security for a corps, if that person received an order from the Main Staff head of security that was at conflict with either an order of his own Corps Commander or corps policy, existing corps policy, which one do you believe under the regulations he would be obliged to obey? He might try to accommodate them, I understand that, and go to the Corps Commander and explain his dilemma, but if push came to shove, which one does he owe primary obedience to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My readings of the JNA Corps Command Regulations and the JNA Security Regulations, both being adopted by the VRS, those are -- that's very specific. It notes that the security, the assistant commander for security and the security organ work for, are answerable to, and under the command of the Corps Commander -- or the Commander of that echelon. If we're referring to the assistant commander for security of a corps, he is under the command of and responsible to primarily the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So if he should receive a proposed order or directive from the Main Staff, chief of security, with whom he does have communication lines, as you explained, that ran counter to his own commander's orders or to what he believed to be command corps policy, then he would have a duty, certainly, as I understand it, to go talk to his corps commander about it and attempt to resolve the dilemma, unless it was an investigation of personal malfeasance as you said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now you talked some about the duty of investigating war crimes that a Commander had under the existing regulations here which, as I understand it, would include the duty to make inquiries or investigations, if there were enough evidence or suspect evidence to suggest that these might be being committed. Would a Chief of Staff have that same duty, that same level of duty? Or if a Chief of Staff had some evidence that came before him to suggest that there might be war crimes going or crimes against the international norms of war going on, would his duty be to go talk to the Commander or to initiate some kind of investigation on his own?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer that in two parts, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part is as codified in the SFRY regulations, and as I previously discussed, I won't go into detail. There are three broad categories of liability under those regulations: the individual liability, the superior, and, of course, the under orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff by position within the entire corps structure does not just qualify as any officer. He is, by position, the second senior ranking officer in the entire corps. If he finds out about it, in the sense where he finds out about this, on his own authority as the Chief of Staff and the Deputy Commander, he would certainly have the authority to phone down to the brigade or to whatever level and order the operation to cease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Or to at least find out --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if he were to operate under the presumption that the corps commander was doing this without the knowledge of the Chief of Staff, as the Chief of Staff finds out about this, and again in a theoretical sense, gives the order to stop, the brigade commander is going to accept that order at face value, operating under the assumption that the Chief of Staff was authorised to give it anyway. So even in a theoretical sense where there was a gigantic conspiracy to cut him out of the loop, once he found out, he certainly had within his own discretion the powers to at least take some form of action against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You said at one point I think that there was no specific evidence that the shelling of Srebrenica when -- during the takeover targeted the civilian population as such. When you used the word "targeted" in both your question and answer, did you mean simply that there was no evidence that the shelling, the shells, were aimed directly at people, or did you also include the motion that perhaps the shells might be used to, in a word, terrorise or scare people into certain modes of action, even though they weren't aimed at, you know, physically injuring those people?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, the comment that I made, and I did qualify it in my testimony, was that I have no specific evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the VRS and the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, clearly Dutch witnesses have testified that they believe that the civilians were, in fact, being shelled. When I talk about the issue of targeting, and again looking at it from a very narrow military sense --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- what I'm looking for is evidence or information that the shell was aimed at or the round was aimed at a specific location or with that specific intent. Now, I understand that that is a very narrow view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So in other words, your answer was not ruling out, that's all I wanted to -- the notion that you might also use shelling as a strategic way of getting civilian population to move on, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. And as I believe some of the Dutch have testified, their impression was that as the civilian column was moving up the road, the shell pattern that they observed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- certainly inferred that to them, that they were being herded in a direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Tell me if you're able to answer this question based upon the information base that you have: Would you say in the almost complete evacuation of the Muslim population from Srebrenica, that the dominant factors -- or how would you rate the factors of, one, the actions of the VRS in taking over the town militarily; two, the decision by the military and perhaps civilian leaders of the BiH at a certain point that they thought it was best for them to move on to Potocari; and three, just the spontaneous reactions of the population itself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to the sequence of events between the military operation at Srebrenica and the BiH activities, clearly as indicated by one of the exhibits I believe the Defence raised, by the 9th of July, the BiH military and civilian leadership in Srebrenica realised that, one, the UN forces were not going to be able to prevent the VRS from taking the town; and two, that they militarily themselves could not do that and were awaiting guidance. Certainly as Colonel Karremans discusses the next day or that evening in his discussions, he discusses the issue of the fact that NATO, to his understanding, will conduct airstrikes sometime on the 11th. That evening of the 10th, for whatever reason, the BiH military and civilian leadership does not believe that or does not believe that that's going to be enough to effect that, and that's where you get the first series of events from the BiH side, the population movement. The civilians going into town and then clustering at the UN enclave or at the UN base, and then the military population and the military-age men, population to attempt to break out to what is known as free territory. After that, with regards to the BiH and their governmental policy or whatever, I did not analyse that because relative to the limited goals of what I was asked to do, that didn't become relevant after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. My next question deals with the column. We had a couple of discussions about how the VRS was entitled under military law to treat a mixed military-civilian column as a military target of some sort. We also had in your report, testimony, that actually the number of armed men, at least, it seemed to me the greatest estimate, the highest estimate was about a third of the column, and then there were estimates that were lower than that, that maybe a thousand of these men out of the several thousand that were in the column were armed. Do we know whether or not the armed men were at the head of the column for the breakthrough primarily. Or whether they were scattered at random, as it were, throughout the column? Predicate to that, the second part of the question would be, is it indeed, if they were concentrated at the beginning, if, of the armed column -- of the column, then is it legitimate for the enemy to treat the whole column as a military target if large portions of it are clearly purely civilian? That's kind of a complicated question; do the best you can.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. With regard to my view, and what I'll qualify is, is my view now is going to represent my understanding of what I think the VRS was aware of at certain points in time. Certainly the understanding on the 12th and the 13th during those early days reflects an awareness that there was significant military assets pushed into the front of the column. Also, and as the witness testimony indicates, there were armed soldiers throughout the length, but certainly the bulk of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Was at the front.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was at the front of the column. As that column then transited through the zone of the Zvornik Brigade the 14th, 15th, and 16th, clearly intelligence reports that the VRS is receiving from their sources qualify the column in a series of one, two, or three groups, either an advanced group, a reconnaissance group, and the main body, and they note that the bulk of the fighters are in the beginning of the column. As a matter of record that we've discussed as part of the evidence base, on the 14th of July, Dusko Vukotic, an intelligence officer assigned to the Zvornik infantry brigade, makes a report to the command of the Drina Corps, the intelligence command of the Drina Corps, recommending that some thought should be given, considering the strength of this part of the front of the column, that they be allowed through, and then the remainder of the column can be successfully engaged. And as you look at the series of events that occur afterwards, that is what was reflected on the ground, a temporary truce to allow the bulk of the column that was armed through, a closing of the lines, and then a series of continual sweep operations through the remainder of the zone against the bulk of the column which, by the 15th -- by the 17th and the 18th, surely there must have been an understanding that they were either poorly armed or not armed at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
