utterances.text: But there was nothing militarily illegitimate about that. Even if you only have a scattering of arms in a predominantly civilian column, it's still okay to treat it as a military target?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best that I can do on that is to again refer back to the fact that under their reading of that specific portion of the regulation on a mixed civilian military target, that at a broad level, it's acceptable. However, there is a qualification that military commanders, in doing so, are required to take due regard to the military benefits of the military operations and how they would impact either the civilian population or, in this case, whether or not the casualties that the civilians would occur in a pocket of people justifies the military necessity. And in that regard, judgements on that would be legally speculative and probably above my purview, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: You gave us your elaboration both in your report and in your oral testimony about why you think it would be permissible, perhaps even necessary, to infer from the facts that General Krstic actually became operationally the Commander a day or two days -- a day before President Karadzic's appointment, and two days, I think, before it was to be effective, and you made out that case, which we don't have to go into. On the other hand, if I understand your answers correctly, and this is why, to several of the questions dealing with the possibility that the Defence raised that the Commander-in-Chief of the whole force, General Mladic, might have taken charge of a particular operation or a particular part of the Drina Corps responsibility; namely, while Krstic is fighting the war in Zepa, the theory might have been that Mladic says, "You just take care of Zepa, and I'll take care of the operations in Bratunac Zvornik Brigade." You raised several reasons, I think, why you thought that was not probably a plausible scenario, because there was no formal reallocation of the authority and the commanders while he remained the formal Commander, retain the responsibility, even if other operations were going on in his domain. I'm wondering if you might explain a little bit more why you think that, in fact, one couldn't imply the same kind of well-operationally-it-was-done approach towards a possible scenario. I understand if you say there isn't enough evidence that that happened, but could it have happened in an informal fashion, Mladic saying, "The Main Staff is going to handle this, and you just take care of Zepa"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two parts to that question. I'd like to answer one, and I think I can answer it in open, and the other one I would request going into a closed session on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. You can save the closed session maybe till the end and we'll do everything in one closed, so just answer the open-session part.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just write down the -- with regards to the second part, the issue pertaining to Mladic and the Main Staff going to handle that aspect and allowing just the Drina Corps element to handle Zepa, one, from a practical aspect, again remembering the workload, that the entire country is at war and there are six VRS corps all conducting combat operations just not one in isolation, certainly in July of 1995, the issues pertaining to the ultimate military operations with regard to the entry of the Croatian army proper into the war -- we call that Operation Storm -- in late July, early August, took a lot of assets and resources and time and energy from the Main Staff to a point where General Mladic's deputy, Colonel -- or General Lieutenant Colonel Milovanovic, was for the most part operating out of a Main Staff forward headquarters in Banja Luka, to deal primarily with a lot of the important issues that came out of there. Sarajevo military operations were occurring at the same time, as well as operations in other areas. So from a workload-intensive look only, to ask the Main Staff to take not only their burden but essentially take on the entire burden of a corps headquarters, it would certainly almost double their workload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But my question is -- I understand that. That's your reason why. On the facts it's not likely to have happened, but the fact is we do have evidence on the public record that General Mladic was sighted on several of those places where some of these holding actions and even where some of the executions were taking place. So we know that he was down there, we know that some of his Main Staff was down there, and I guess my basic question is: Could he have, under existing military regulations or military law have said, "I'm going to take charge of this. I'll use your Drina Corps assets down that. I'll use some of your Drina Corps people and equipment and everything else, but you take care of Zepa, and I'm going to take charge. I'm down there, I'll be on the site, et cetera."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the larger sense, as the Commander of the army of Republika Srpska, he does that anyway. On the other aspects, certainly we have him on the ground on the 12th and the 13th of July. We have him in Belgrade on the evening of the 14th and all day on the 15th, according to General Elliot's affidavit. So at a point in time, his physical presence disappears. Now, that certainly doesn't imply that his ability to command and control disappears. He -- certainly there are Main Staff officers in the zone of the Drina Corps, but it would again come back to the observations of the size and scale and scope of the operation. Certainly it would be at the direction of General Mladic. The question then becomes: How did he choose to execute that? And again, General Mladic, being an experienced commander and staff officer, it would be difficult for me to believe that for the purposes, that he would essentially remove one or two or five of the most critical officers of the corps and isolate them completely, and then of his own violation or volition try to handle it himself. I mean, in essence, to do that, he is degrading his own abilities to successfully conduct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I have just about four, I think, rapid questions. One, we heard one theory raised in some of the Defence questions that the references to the word, which I don't -- couldn't pronounce correctly, for burial, in a couple of the excepts, might have referred, or at least this was the inference I drew from the question, might have referred to the normal kind of cleaning up of a battleground after you've had a battle, and I'm wondering whether or not you thought that was logical given the description of the kinds of equipment we saw moving around and being requisitioned for whatever it was being requisitioned for.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, perhaps the best way to do it is keeping in mind the time sequence of the events as they occurred. The phrase itself obviously refers to the burial of bodies. It doesn't qualify how the bodies got there. What I tried to do as part of my analysis is to go to the effort of quantifying where the combat from the column was physically and where it occurred in time, and then demonstrate that based on the times that we see the engineer equipment operating, that there cannot be a physical linkage between the two. I mean, in the sense of Colonel Pandurevic as a Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I would find it very difficult for him to be concerned about the burial of bodies on a battlefield, from a battlefield context, before the battle has really gotten underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I've just got four questions now. If the Main Staff was running an operation of any sort in the Corps Commander's territory without there having been a formal recertification or reallocation of authority, would it be the normal military procedure for the Commander, for the Corps Commander, to be told about both that operation and some degree of detail? In other words, just hypothesise that the Main Staff said, "We'll take care of the treatment of the prisoners as they move into Bratunac," and just hypothesise that. Would it be the normal military procedure that the Corps Commander would be told that and also told at least the outlines of the plan for their treatment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, ma'am. The fundamental issue within a military structure, particularly a ground army, is that everybody has to know what everybody's doing. I mean, certainly not the individual soldier on the ground, but the staff, because it is their job to, one, coordinate the activities, and to further deconflict [sic] the activities. Because, again, in a live-fire environment, if everybody is not clear where soldiers are on the ground, you will end up killing your own people. We've done that in various wars in the US Army. It's not an exact science, and a lot of the work of the staff resolves around that. The second piece is again from a military aspect and as demonstrated by what occurred in the Zvornik Brigade, at the same time these events are occurring, you've got significant military activity, and you have a conflict in the resources required to either fight the column or to bury the bodies and conduct the executions. And again, with Colonel Pandurevic noting that there is a conflict here, he needs guidance, he needs reinforcements, it's an unexpected situation, and the manifestation of this command and staff activity to get Colonel Pandurevic the tools he needs to both fight the column and continue on the execution process. I mean, that's why the system works the way it does, and that's why it's -- particularly within the JNA and former VRS, orders that are issued at one level are normally reviewed by the next superior level just so everyone up the chain is aware of what is occurring, in detail, why it's occurring, in detail, what resources will be needed so the decisions can be made to execute the plans knowing everything that goes behind the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Exhibit 619, which I believe is -- the Defence counsel brought up again, which is an order from the Main Staff to the Drina command and the recipients, several of the brigade commanders which you -- brigade commands which you discussed, but I noticed, in looking at the heading on that, when it said, "Drina command, from the Main Staff," it says, "for information," and then it says, "Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade." Is there any -- I mean, it says "Drina Corps command," then "for information." It's unclear to me, reading the English translation, if the "for information" is for the Drina command, if the "for information" is for the following -- the individual brigade commands. Do you have any impression on that? Or is it completely random?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to discuss this a little in direct. It is a bit confusing because of the language issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, in that particular exhibit, unless I'm mistaken, if you go to the B/C/S version, behind it you will see where the comma is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or "for information," and then units listed behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: From which you would infer what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the order was directed to the higher command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And the information was down below.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in some of our discussions with other VRS officers, they indicate that generally while it is a rare practice that occurs, it is a practice that does occur and it is indicative of the fact that the higher command wants to make sure that everybody is on the same sheet of paper and it wants to do so in a timely manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now my last question, but it's a little bit complicated. At various times, people, and we don't -- I mean, have suggested that may have been a plan from the very beginning about the treatment of the prisoners, namely, the women and children would go on through to Kladanj and the men would not. But the time line, and maybe you can go over this for me briefly -- and there's also been evidence very early on, maybe it was even the 12th but it may have been the 13th, you suggested that people down the line had to be going around finding these holding stations like these schools and the various places so they would be ready when the prisoners arrived. On the other hand, we know that the -- in Potocari, the maximum number of men that anybody has suggested there were 900 or 1.000, something like that, from the Potocari group, whereas the bulk of the people that eventually were held in these stations and executed came out of the column. It's my understanding. So I'm trying to get it straight as to whether or not you think, based on the evidence you have, when they were going around finding these holdings stations and that sort of thing, they were doing it just on the basis of the Potocari, because you point out it was the day or so before they caught on what was happening to the column and the capturing began, all of which comes to my final question. If, if there was any kind of plan, was it a static plan or do we have a situation where there may have been originally a plan for a certain number of people, and when a new event like the column came into being, that plan was constantly being adjusted as it went along, that they didn't necessarily know on the first day if there was a plan, what was going to happen on the third or the fourth day to the people from the columns, that those decisions were being made on the spot?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best way that -- or possibly the way that I use, I won't say "best," to try and come to grips with that on a time line of looking back at what a plan might have been, and again keeping in mind that it takes them a few days for the column to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- get established in their mind where it's going and what it's doing, is again when an awareness of -- that there would have been men in Potocari evening of the 11th, the morning of the 12th. Certainly the evening of the 11th the decision was made to start busing them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presumption is that sometime during the evening, the early morning hours of the 12th, somebody in Bratunac started designating and identifying sites to hold individuals who would start arriving by the 12th, by the afternoon of the 12th, the earliest ones. Excuse me. General Mladic makes the statement pertaining to a formal vetting process in his mind for war criminals. The separation at Potocari there, the fact that there's a list, the fact that Dutch witnesses say that in the white house there were photographs out where some people were vetting these individuals, and then again the witnesses describing a widespread practice of the burning and the taking and the confiscation of identification material, which would support that process. The fact that the brutalisation that occurs to these people in the holding facilities in Bratunac infers that they were not given instructions that these people were to either be protected or held, and on another extreme could lead one to interfere that the individuals carrying these out could do so secure in the knowledge that they weren't going to be held accountable for their individual actions, even in the case where you have deaths occurring in the tens, and if one looks at the casualties that occur, the deaths that occur in the hangar, perhaps even in the hundreds, that there is no liability. The troops are doing this at the lowest level with impunity, either -- somehow operating under an assumption that nothing's going to happen to them, despite the presence of their lower-level commanders in and around the area. The -- that piece begins to manifest itself as early as the 12th. Now, again, going under the understanding that perhaps General Mladic and the Drina Corps don't -- they know there are men in Potocari, they don't know how many men, but again they're expecting to find them in the Badara Triangle. So there is no way to say that it wouldn't have been part of that plan at any point in time. And in fact, how flexible it was was the fact that even though they were picked up in a separate location, they were still brought in and held, one, in some of these facilities, those same facilities; and, two, when the facilities were filled up, they were held in bus and trucks outside of those facilities. So certainly the facilities were not filled by the afternoon of the 13th from just by Potocari people, some of these were being filled by people from the column. So again, inferring back, those were the designated sites regardless of where the men were picked up. The great unknown is what they would have estimated the size of the column or the size or the sheer number of men that they were picking up. The other part of the unknown is: At what point in time the Supreme Commanders in that case, in this case General Mladic, came to a decision, either on his own or with the president, or certainly came to the decision that, "We can't -- either we're not going to hold them. We're going to kill them. And we can't kill them here. We have to move them to remote site." Because looking at the overall context of events -- I mean, certainly from the perspective of the army and the perspective of the political and civilian leadership of VRS, considering the broad scale of events as they're occurring, it is hard to envision a better bargaining chip in dealing with the political authorities of certainly the BiH government and of the International Community than having 10.000 to 15.000 Muslim men in the middle of Potocari in a legitimate prisoner of war facility under the control or under the supervision of certainly the UN troops that were there and the ICRC at a point in time. That is the ultimate bargaining chip, to be able to get significant political leverage from people, one would think, and this chip was thrown away for another reason. And again, I don't know what that reason could be. So going back in the series of time as to when the plan expanded from hold them into these facilities and kill them while they're in these facilities to remove them to a more remote zone, the best that I can infer on that is the Zvornik Brigade or elements of the Zvornik brigade became aware of that plan sometime on the 13th, and the reflection of that is how it was manifested or manifested in the travels of those vehicles looking for potential sites. Again, as the Defence raised, most of these sites were in remote locations, with the exception of the Pilica Dom. And again going back to the sheer number of people, the Orahovac facility filled up, the Petkovci facility filled up, the Pilica facility filled up, possibly the school at Rosevic filled up. The people are still -- again, as a military operation, it's not just a tap that turns on and off. Buses are still moving up the road and they've got to put them somewhere. They put them in Pilica Dom. But just to finish the last part of the question as to where the intent was, it can't be forgotten that the first of the large-scale executions doesn't occur in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, it occurs in the Cerska Valley belonging to, I believe, the Milici Brigade, as early as noon on 13 July. And when you look at the external components of that, it was organised insomuch as there were buses carrying the men. They had a military escort, and behind those buses or as part of those buses there was earth-moving equipment. It wasn't a holding site they were going to up the valley to in Cerska. It was not a convenient place to hold them. This is where they were going to be executed. And again, the reflections of conversations in some of the intercepts where Drina Corps staff officers, as early as the afternoon of 13 July, are looking for engineer equipment. So in my mind, that is the first manifestation of a major move, that it's not ones and twos, it's tens [sic] any more, it's a systematic process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. I see that it is 20 to 1. I, too, have a large number of questions for you, so if we begin with my questions, we will be under pressure because we will need a closed session, so perhaps it would be better to have a break, at least for me to prepare my questions. I have asked the registrar to prepare the exhibits which I intend to use, and to facilitate your answers. My questions will be very simple, but maybe your answers will not, so I'm going to ask Madam Registrar to put before Mr. Butler the exhibits. So we're going to have a break. I think 20 minutes will suffice because after that we don't have much more to do. 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, I am going to ask you a certain number of questions, 14 in all; some have subquestions to them. I proceed from the principle that all my questions require answers from you after you have reviewed and read all these documents. Some are hypothetical, but they are always based on the information you acquired having read and reviewed all these documents, and they also rely on your expertise and your military experience and knowledge. I am starting from Exhibit 409 which perhaps you have in front of you, and the question is the following: The Corps Commander, can he decide without telling his assistant commander, that is, the Chief of Staff, about it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may very well -- depending on the order, there may be instances where that is theoretically possible. A very simplistic order may be an individual type of an order. But within the realistic scheme of how a military command and staff works, trying to do that on a broader scale and trying to keep the Chief of Staff specifically out of the loop very quickly runs the risk of military confusion, particularly if it's an order that would require the work of subordinates on the staff to have to accomplish, and yet somehow not be able to do that, deal with the Chief of Staff and then deal directly through the Commander. I mean, one of the last issues on the command is the fact that the one resource a Commander can't fix on the battlefield and can't somehow modify or alter is time. He's got a lot of missions and a lot of jobs and a lot of hard decisions, and he has "X" amount of time. And one of the reasons why he has the Chief of Staff and the staff is so he can give a simple order or broad guidance and not himself have to spend the hours necessary taking that broader guidance and turning it into specific executable tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any indications of the presence of Arkan's Tigers in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I understand from one or two witness statements that an individual is identified either as a member of the Arkan group or is seen wearing an Arkan Tiger uniform or distinctive patch; but from my review of the document base in question, I have no information which would support that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if we take into consideration Exhibits 423 and 424, those exhibits refer to regular units, if I can call them that; and in connection with that you said that at a given moment, paramilitary units were integrated into the regular structure or were disbanded. How can we interpret their presence in the context of military principles?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With that regard, I believe I qualified that "that moment in time" was in mid to late 1992. The physical presence of a single individual is not something that in isolation, that I would say qualifies the presence of that individual to the fact that a paramilitary unit is fully there. What I'm looking for as part of my analysis to come to grips with that issue is information or evidence which would suggest that either multiple sightings which we could use or which I would use to refer multiple individuals, or some evidence within the documents or within other statements that I could use as an additional piece of evidence coming from another source to confirm or deny that. And at the end of the day, what I've come up with is I have this specific statement, and I just have no other information which would allow me to confirm or deny their physical presence. I can't say that they were there; I cannot say that they weren't there. I cannot confirm it, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 425 mentions repeatedly UNPROFOR and the International Community and international public opinion. Do you have any idea as to, and I have two subquestions, the role that these factors played in the decisions taken by the responsible officials of the army of Republika Srpska, and what was the understanding of those factors or perception of those factors by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to Srebrenica in 1995 in that regards, certainly the army, as well as the civilian leadership of the country Republika Srpska, was very aware and had to take those into consideration. The manifestation of that in my mind, of how they took those considerations into effect, first would be the Krivaja-95 OP plan itself which does not specify the taking of the town of Srebrenica as an objective; the 5 July 1995 air defence order published by the Drina Corps, a reflection that because of the upcoming operations, NATO aircraft would potentially be involved, understanding that they would expect some reaction out of the UN as a result of the increased military operations; the fact that when you look at the scope of the operations, and I have to give them very good credit on this, it was very much done, at least from my view, not in a way that would immediately cause a trigger to be tripped in the International Community or with the UN. It was a very slow, cautious approach, moving forward, taking an OP, moving forward again, taking an OP, working very hard not to cause UN casualties as reflected in some cases by the way they did this. In other cases, you know, firing at the UN, always a pattern or a lack of pattern that the UN and the International Community could grasp onto as the ultimate intent. And clearly, the lack of response or the lack of perceived response was a factor in the 9 July 1995 order in the name of President Karadzic to expand the goal of the operation. So again, throughout the course of the operation, the actual military part, they were very cognizant of the International Community and the UN. That same type of recognition is also reflected in many ways by the way the prisoners were handled afterwards: The conscious effort to move the men out of the eyesight of the Dutch who were there; the plan, as it was perceived from the results of the observations of the Dutch, that their vehicles were being taken away, and that their ability to monitor the events in the name of the UN and the International Community was being systematically degraded; the fact that even in Bratunac, the understanding that there was still too much of the International Community there between relevant UN forces that were in Bratunac at the Hotel Fontana, between the ICRC and other international organisations, and even an awareness that's reflected in the conversation between Miroslav Dzuronic, the civilian commissioner for refugees, and the office of the president which, as I reviewed now -- I wasn't sure yesterday -- took place on 13 July with the instructions of "get them out of there." And in essence, they're moved to the isolated locations which would not reasonably be expected to be under anyone's view. And certainly as the army operation that everyone could watch was moving from Srebrenica to the UN operation in Zepa, certainly the International Community and the UN's view was focussed on that, as well as being focussed on having to deal with the thousands and tens of thousands of Muslim civilians, women and children, coming out of Kladanj. So at a higher level than just a military level, certainly an awareness that everything that they did would somehow have to be conducted with regards to what the UN and what the International Community could see and would believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 428 refers to the separation and reduction of the enclaves as the objectives of the military operations as a first step, at the same time, the creation of conditions for the elimination of those enclaves. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those objectives, were they separate or were they simultaneous in time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- well, from a military sequence, separated by time one after the other. In a planning sequence, they were certainly looked at as a unified plan, and we see the manifestation of that in some of the 9 and 10 July -- matter of fact, I believe there's 10 July Drina Corps order that is either an exhibit or part of my supporting material which reflects the fact that as a result of what is occurring at Srebrenica, we're now in a position to start taking advantage of that and start setting the conditions for the military operation at Zepa. So while the military events fall in sequence because you need the same forces and they can't be in two places at once, the planning intent was certainly together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If one assesses the results, do the results coincide with the objectives, or is there a discrepancy between the two, and if so, what is the discrepancy between the objectives and the results achieved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe from a military sense, the results exceeded the planned objectives but met the modified objective insomuch as the fact that the initial intent and goals was, first, the physical reduction of the enclave, and to create the conditions where presumably the United Nations and the International Community would evacuate the enclave. In effect, try to replay what happened in 1993 prior to the establishment of the enclave. In that regard where I think they were surprised was from a military sense, they were surprised by their success, and a lot of the events that you see relative to the frenzy of activity trying to get the buses and the resources to move the population is a reflection of the fact that it didn't occur to them until almost the 11th, the evening of the 11th, that they would need to do that. I mean, looking at a corps staff and any military staff, part of that process is to be able to anticipate events so you can plan for them before you need whatever you need. And in this regard, you don't see that. There was no prior planning for that aspect. So from a military sense, they did achieve that at the low end. At the larger end, they achieved the goals of what they wanted, which was the elimination of Srebrenica and Zepa as enclaves, and in a larger sense, now they did not have those two enclaves to deal with in the area of the wider area of the Predendija [phoen] Valley. Now, going to the next step of whether that included Gorazde and whether they thought they could get away with that as well is a bit speculative based on the information that I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that in the original plan, the evacuation of the population was included, was envisaged?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we referring to the original OP plan Krivaja-95? I don't read it as such. The specific line that I believe you're referring to would be part of the procedures that would be relative -- and, again, I don't want to put words in your mouth, sir, but I believe this is the passage that you would be referring to, the issue of dealing with prisoners in a war in a civilian population behaving in every way. When I look at that, I don't take that to mean that they are already thinking through the process of removing thousands of numbers of individuals. I believe we're referring here to something of a much smaller scale. The fact that they can anticipate that they're going to take a number of prisoners, certainly at the beginning of the operation in maybe ones and maybe tens, that they're going to come across members of the civilian population, and as previous testimony has indicated, there was, in fact, a rather large civilian project out there, I believe it's called the Swedish Shelter Project, in that area, so it would not be unreasonable at all to expect that their combat troops would be dealing with prisoners of war and civilians in that aspect of the combat. But I wouldn't take this any further than that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if we come to the 11th or the 12th of July, specifically to the meetings held in the Fontana Hotel, I don't know whether it would be naive to say that there was an intention on the part of those responsible to evacuate the population. But what we know today is that persons were executed. I don't know whether we can see there a change of orientation. And if so, what could have been the reasons that led to the executions when, after all, they were always talking about evacuation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, based on the events and probably the best trigger of the event in my mind that would illustrate that intent would be at the first meeting and then further at the second meeting. At the first meeting, General Mladic articulates he wants to see the Muslim military commanders; second meeting, the same. He doesn't know that the 28th Division is trying to escape. Again, their understanding is that that division is in the Bandera Triangle to the south-west of Srebrenica and may be preparing to fight or may be preparing to make an escape towards Zepa. He doesn't know that they're going out as a column or that there is an intent. It's almost clear, at least in my mind, that on the evening of 11th July, General Mladic, by that first meeting, second meeting, he's looking to set the conditions for a set peace surrender of the 28th Division to him. Somewhere after that second meeting and through the events that are occurring late in the evening of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, as his tactical units on the ground along those roads start indicating that there's a column moving, there is an awareness that, one, the 28th Infantry Division is not where the VRS thought it was; and, two, that the 28th Infantry Division is not going to surrender but is, in effect, trying to organise a mass escape and return to the lines of the BiH. If I had to say what is the event where the light turned on or the light turned off, I would say that recognition by General Mladic that that event that he expected, that he was going to gain custody of those people, again perhaps for a potential bargaining chip or for whatever reasons, was not going as he had anticipated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibits 437 and 445 speak about the mobilisation of buses and also of drivers. You may have already answered this question, but I would like to insist upon it. This mobilisation, was it part of the initial plan or of the modified or adjusted plan, following what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, given the fact that the VRS, in general, and certainly the corps tried to be as organised as possible and predict major events like this, certainly where large numbers of resources are going to be used, all of the activity pertaining to buses and pertaining to the resources to move the population appear, in my view, to be reactive to the situation that's occurring. They're not in anticipation of an event. We don't see, prior to the early morning hours of 12 July, any thought process whatsoever on the side of the army or even the side of the civilian government that they would have to do this. When you look at that and other statements that are taken in the context of the events, it almost appears that until the late evening hours of the 11th, the early morning hours of the 12th, they had always perceived that the UN would do this and not them, and that it would be the UN that would gather the assets, it would be the UN that would actually use all the resources, particularly the large number of buses and the large amount of fuel that would do this, that would have to come out of the very limited coffers of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we come to Exhibit 459. The treatment given to civilians mentioned in the postscript, is it possible to make a distinction between the envisaged treatment and the other treatment that was, in fact, given?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the key qualifier in this specific paragraph is the recognition of how it will be necessary to present the operation in Srebrenica to the media. They're qualifying the public face and the private face. I don't think, at this point in time -- I mean, again, they're qualifying it. We have to advance the perception that here's the treatment of the civilians and even here's the treatment of surrendered soldiers. This is the public scene. So this is, in my mind, not an awareness of a duality of how they're going to treat the individuals but an awareness of the fact that "what we do and what we sell publicly has to be different."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be said that they were playing with public opinion in a sense, that in a way they were lying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I believe that the fact basis supports that they were manipulating the public opinion or attempting to. The fact that we have the 12 July order that specifies that access to foreign media, foreign information sources is going to be restricted along those closed highways and that only media under the accompaniment of the army -- and again, the media coverage by Zoran Petrovic, typical of that -- would be allowed to put the best public face on. I mean, certainly we know there were at least three media outlets taping events there. We know that Zoran Petrovic; we know that Colonel Milovanovic, who was the RS press information officer, it's his footage, is my understanding, where we have the video footage of the meetings; and there was another film camera down there as well showing Mladic on the 12th in Potocari. So certainly within this aspect, they are attempting to present the best possible public light to the events both as they're occurring and after the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go back to the Zoran Petrovic interview, has this question something to do with the statement, that is Exhibit 499, according to which, and I'm going to quote it in English [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "peripheral phenomenon in war." Is there a relationship between the two? This statement is found on page 2, paragraph 5, "Refugees are a peripheral phenomenon in war."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, and again not reflecting the views of the author on this one, I think he's accurately recounting the fact that military combat, military conflict, does not occur in isolation with the civilian population. I mean, in fact, with regret, most of the combat seems to occur there. Very rarely do you get the situation where you have the luxury of a wide open desert with very little civilian population issues to deal with. Civilians or noncombatants always attempt to flee. I mean, it's a phenomenon, it's a known one, it's a rational choice, and military forces have been having to deal with the aspects of civilian populations and what that means in their military operations before, during, and afterwards for as long as I've been reading military history. It is a phenomenon of war. It's a recognised phenomenon of war. It doesn't occur in isolation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 433 refers, among other things, to the presence of General Mladic. I think we have already discussed this at some length, but maybe this is from a slightly different angle. Is it normal for the Major General, the chief of the command, to be present in these conditions? And if not, what are the reasons that you would give for his presence there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly given the perception that we're on the eve of a major Serbian VRS victory, I would certainly expect General Mladic to be there. As I've noted in my previous testimony, particularly with relation to the video footage of the walkthrough of Srebrenica with General Krstic and General Zivanovic, one of the fundamental tenets of leadership and command is to be seen doing that. General Mladic is the commander of the army of Republika Srpska. That's not an esoteric position that is done in isolation. As a commander at any level -- and I believe this is a pretty universal military concept -- the commander has to be out with the troops and to be seen being with the troops, sharing the hardships, sharing the rewards. He has to be seen commanding and being seen leading. If you look at the video footage of General Mladic through the war, he makes very sure that there are video cameras around making sure he is seen doing all of those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you come across any pieces of information which could lead you to have some views regarding the relationship, even personal relationship, between General Mladic and the Drina Corps, and more specifically, with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The professional association with General Mladic and General Zivanovic, and where I believe it crosses over to a personal level, goes back as far as I can track it with the material I have before the war, at least the war in Bosnia, where General Mladic was the commander of the JNA 9th Corps in Knin, and where General Zivanovic was one of his brigade commanders, the Commander of the 180th Motorised Brigade, I believe. When the war begins, General Mladic, of course, becomes the Commander of the Main Staff of the newly-formed army of Republika Srpska. And one of his deputies -- and if my information is correct, the Main Staff Chief of Artillery during the early period of 1992 was then Colonel Zivanovic. Again, a continued professional relationship. The fact that in November 1992, when the Drina Corps is formed, General Zivanovic is appointed to be the Commander of that corps. One would presume that while it would be President Karadzic who appoints the Corps Commander because it's a general position, that he would have done so with the endorsement and on the recommendation of General Mladic. Their continued professional association over the three years of the course of conflict, and because of the evidence base, I can't really qualify that in too much depth, until General Zivanovic leaves. And perhaps the last piece is the actions or the activities of General Zivanovic after he leaves. I mean, upon his retirement, he is, in fact, promoted to the rank of Lieutenant Colonel-General as he retires. So I can certainly catalogue a long professional relationship in a superior/subordinate relationship, a very close one, between General Mladic and General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now come to a subject which was already addressed by my distinguished colleague Judge Riad. It has to do with the question why General Zivanovic was replaced by General Krstic. You have already touched upon that question, but I would like to come back to it with this question: Is it possible to think that General Zivanovic was perhaps not in agreement with the plan or the attitude of General Mladic in that operation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is a definite possibility and one of the two or three theories that we hold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 446, I think that in the analysis that you have made of this exhibit I'm talking about Exhibit number 446 --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that in front of me, sir. I have 464 not 446. Oh, here it is on the bottom, sir. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So this exhibit, according to your analysis, refers to the first convoy of women and children that left Potocari. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time frame of 1305 and 12 July supports that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that point, that is, the 12th of July at 1305 hours, was it possible for General Krstic to be informed of the execution or of a plan of executions, and if yes, why and how can we make that conclusion that he was aware of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we -- or in my case, if I make the assumption that that plan occurred sometime between the second meeting on 11 July and the third meeting on 12 July, the physical presence of General Krstic at both those meetings and in the Bratunac area during the period leads me to believe if there was a plan of that nature, he would have known about that. Now, looking at this specific intercept pertaining to the buses, one would make the inference that part of that would be the knowledge that the women, the women -- and maybe the best way to do it would be to say those people who didn't qualify as military combatants or potential military combatants were not part of that plan. One of the unique things that I can use that helps me to support that theory is witness testimony that was brought before the Court earlier where on 13 July in the Sandici meadow, there was an awareness that they were looking to exclude out of the groups of people individuals who were not between the ages of 16 and 60. And that was an awareness by the soldiers at the lowest level. So in that regards, the intent that there's a plan, that there's the intent that there was some form of thought process who will be excluded from that group manifests itself in both this intercept and in that other piece of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. Butler, if Mladic knew about this -- and we have information, but now I ask you the questions. I will present this to you conditionally as a question. So if Mladic did know about the executions, would it be normal to think that Krstic knew about it, too?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first question, did Mladic know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The physical presence, as noted by a lot of the witnesses, and the physical -- and the descriptions and the statements by them, as well as the footage of him in Potocari on 12 July, and certainly his presence on 13 July on the Bratunac road up to Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, and the bodies that are on the road during that period, and in one specific instance, that there was one individual killed at Sandici that I believe is closely associated with his presence, strongly infers that; but I can't based on that alone say that from those events, that Mladic knew. I mean, that's a mental state judgement that I can't make, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 459, please. I will quote in English, [In English] "... has stayed in the hospital of Bratunac at the request of the hospital staff to make sure that the patients are properly treated. I intend to send him away tomorrow under the pretext that his help is not necessary." [Interpretation] Taking into account the fact that there seem to be two entities making decisions and two criteria for the decision making, what are your comments? And perhaps I can ask another question. Do you have any indications about the fate of the 57 wounded, the 18 persons that were relocated later, and some five or six people who died in the hospital in Bratunac? Who were dying, not the persons who actually died, but who were dying.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's easier to answer the second question first. My understanding from the investigation and dealing with them particularly with regards to this issue, is that they have in fact looked at this closely, and all of the information that we have to date from both the VRS documents as well as from the International Community, the Red Cross and those agencies that actually did monitor the transfer, indicates that for the most part that this group of individuals was in fact properly treated, was in fact evacuated under proper medical supervision, and many of those were in fact taken to the detention centre at Bajkovici; to include, if you look at a related document to this, the fact that Captain 1st Class Nikolic indicates that 23 were transferred on this date under Drina Corps military police guidance, and one person was given to the municipal police as a confessed war criminal. And even he comes out after the war from the camp at Bajkovici. So with this regard, my understanding is that the investigation, while certainly continuing in this regard, has not yet determined anything to date that would warrant further action. In answer to your second question, again, you've reflected on the fact that Colonel Radislav Jankovic, the intelligence officer or unintelligence [sic] officer of the Main Staff, is making an intention or informing both the Drina Corps and the Main Staff of his intention to send the doctor away under the pretence that he's no longer needed, again, part of that larger campaign to remove international eyes from the area. Now, certainly in this specific case, either by design or just because there were too many eyes, and I won't speculate as to what the situation was, these people were treated properly. So with that regard, it does seem to be contradictory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But one could think that this person that -- had intention to get rid of the doctor or to no longer use his services, that he asked the hospital staff whether they needed the doctor, that they would have said that they still needed him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interesting parallel, and again if you note it, is that the doctor's -- he stayed on at the hospital at the request of the hospital staff, so presumably some medical authority wants him to stay for whatever reason; and yet, yes, Colonel Jankovic as the intelligence officer is making a pretext to send him away, overriding that medical advice or that medical desire, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibits 463 and 464. In your opinion, these two exhibits are co-related; they need each other. Between the two terms, one that's used in 463 which is "search," and 464, which is "search" -- there seems to be a problem with translation and terminology. Do we need to look up this word in the dictionary. There seems to be the same term used in both documents and the original.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that in this case, I mean, the phrase "search and sweep operation" are used interchangeably. And looking at particularly when you break down the Bratunac Brigade order, what the actual order is directing is a rather coordinated sweep operation, the goal being to, as the military unit passes over the terrain in a somewhat linear fashion, that everything behind that unit is in fact secured. It has no -- they do not leave behind any enemy forces; they do not bypass anybody. It becomes a secure area. So I think in that respect, we are -- we remain functionally talking about the same type of operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 556, we have already visited this exhibit today, [In English] "Take this as an order," 14 July. [Interpretation] My question, perhaps it is repetitious, but it is from a slightly different angle, could this mean that General Zivanovic could have legitimate doubts that his interlocutor does not -- is not aware of the conditions in which the order is given, that it is an order? What I was saying was, that the person he's speaking to does not see it as him being in a position to give orders?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is in fact how I do interpret it, and if -- when at a point in time we go into closed session, I will provide additional information which in fact supports why I interpret it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 564. We have here the dialogue, and I'm referring to page 2, between Malinic who says, [In English] "We should do something to eliminate it," "it" meaning a group. Nastic answers, "yes." And after Malinic, "Can we do that?" [Interpretation] My question, the word "eliminate," does it have a special meaning in military terminology? And let me go on with my other questions. Is it possible to imagine that there was no plan or that there was a plan that some people were aware of and others were not? And finally, can we see that in this document? Were there any surprises or improvisations? I think you already answered that part of my question.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to the first question, certainly in the case of Major Malinic, the Commander of the Military Police Battalion, 65th Protection Regiment, and Major Nastic, the Commander of the Milici Brigade, as senior officials within the structure, the military structure that existed, one in the Drina Corps and one subordinate to the Main Staff, these would, these would be people who would be aware of what was going on if -- as part of the plan. Their assets would be involved in it. They'd have to be aware. The second piece is, and again as you indicate, sir, there is a lot of ad hoc or very rapidly changing military situations or other situations that are presenting themselves, which they have either not fully anticipated or having to react to on a -- in a rapid basis. So in that regard again, yes, this particular intercept reflects that. Going to the last piece based on this, and again Judge Wald, I believe, brought this issue up earlier, what to infer from it, again defaulting back to my statements where that as a military analyst that unless it was clear in my mind what I would infer from it, I would always default back to a potential military meaning. And since I do understand at the period that there was column activity that could have qualified as legitimate, I can make that. However, I certainly can't deny that there is an entirely different way to read this which would lay out criminal intent or certainly criminal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that brings me to Exhibit 712. One can read that: [In English] "General Krstic, this morning, praised the way we have completed our task so far." [Interpretation] Do you have any idea which those tasks were? And another subquestion: What was the date from which they should be included or inserted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question, and in reading this, one has to keep in mind that as the first part notes, "defining task related to coming duties especially at Trnovo," they still were conducting combat operations. Further during this period in time, the Bratunac Brigade or large elements of the Bratunac Brigade were operating under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in Trnovo, that ability to do that, being the fact that the Srebrenica safe area no longer existed. So again, a reflection of a manifestation of that goal. Now we're able to use this brigade in another corps zone. So in this regard, there are potentially a lot of very difficult military operations that occur which, in fact, General Krstic could be praising. At the same time during the period that this is occurring, as the investigation has revealed, we have the process where primary mass burial sites at Glogova, I believe, are being removed and are being reinstalled or moved to the secondary grave sites along the Zeleni Jadar road. And again the comment by Major Nikolic or Captain First Class Nikolic at the back of that is what I take as indicative of that, but I can't necessarily say that the task that General Krstic is praising is or is not related to the second task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned an interview given by General Zivanovic, in which he said that he left the Drina Corps command on the 11th of July. Do you recall the date of that interview?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If memory serves me correctly, that interview was taken in November of 1996. It in fact shows up as a footnote in Mr. David Rhodes' book pertaining to Srebrenica, which is how I found out about it. The interview is not relatively public knowledge because for whatever reason, it was not published by the editors. However, the author has in fact provided the investigation with the completed notes of that interview. But I believe the time is November 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 609. We have revisited that exhibit today, and it has to do with a statement by Vinko Pandurevic. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... "under his responsibility, we will be forced to let them go." [Interpretation] In saying that, is Pandurevic acknowledging that the plans or the plan was not well-adjusted or that there was no plan at all? You have already answered this question in general terms, but more specifically, could it be that Pandurevic either did not know about the plan or that the plan he knew was not adjusted to his needs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to the first part of your question, would I look at this and is this a potential indication of whether or not Colonel Pandurevic knew, and again as I've indicated, the fact that the way he's talking about that is indicative of the fact that he knows there is a plan, and certainly, as a brigade commander coming into his zone again from the Zepa area and very quickly becoming briefed on the situation, he knows how extensive the plan is, he knows what resources are being used, and he also knows that the military situation with the column will require maybe some of those resources to be pulled to another location. So again, I interpret this as reflective of the fact that he understands that there's a plan, and further, he understands that the new military situation that is presenting itself with the column will require reinforcements or modifications to that plan. And when you wrap that in again with the 15 July 1995 intercept conversation between Colonel Beara and General Krstic, Colonel Beara makes it very clear that all of a sudden, because of the situation, people who are supposed to be there or people who he had been counting on earlier are no longer available to execute his portion of that plan presumably to execute Muslim men, and he is rapidly querying the Corps Commander about the availability of additional resources to even qualify the point that, "I will only need them for the day. You can have them back tonight." Clearly again, when you take it in context with the events, a lot of people are suddenly coming to the realisation that plans and resources now have to radically shift to deal with the military situation as it's now presenting itself with the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question for the moment: If we have this column and the evacuation and all the problems related to the column, do you have any information on the conversations between the VRS and the BiH, and do you have any analyses of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intercepts that we have, the BiH intercepts of the VRS communications, reflect the fact that on the ground, that Muslim military commanders or certainly at least one individual who represents himself as a commander, is attempting to make contact with the VRS. We see that reflected in one particular exhibit that I believe was tendered pertaining to a synopsis of a conversation where the individual Semso Muhanovic -- and I'm sure I pronounced his name incorrectly -- is looking for Pandurevic. That individual, Semso, has been in the area of Tuzla for several years as a military commander. Certainly he knows who his opposite number is, and he knows who to contact relative to this, and he does so contact him over a frequency that he knows the VRS is listening to or monitoring, maybe one of their own even. So he does that. Again, a reflection of the 14 July suggestion from Dusko Vukotic, the intelligence officer of the Zvornik Brigade, noting that, "Perhaps we should make contact with them," clearly indicating that contact between the BiH and the VRS, from a military perspective for these things, is certainly not unheard of and may in fact be a channel that occurs relatively frequently, although I can't say that. We certainly know that when we look at the 16 July 1995 daily combat report -- I'm sorry, the interim combat report, that in that report, Colonel Pandurevic notes that because of the military situation and because of what he perceives to be a lack of support, that he, on his own volition, has met with or at least verbally communicated with the Muslim military commanders on the ground there and arranged for a temporary truce to occur. So certainly we have the intent or the idea at the beginning. We have contacts from the Muslim side attempting to make that happen. And even backing off that, we have, on the 9th of July, we have the request from the civilian and military leadership in Srebrenica that the BiH governmental level should initiate contacts with the VRS to see if something like this can be arranged. So certainly intent on both sides, and we see the manifestations of that intent reflected in reality on the 15th and 16th of July, which then leads for at least a portion of the column to leave the territory of VRS and go to BiH territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me, Mr. Butler -- I don't know where I came across that -- that the difference in the negotiations was that on the Muslim side, the condition was for the military and civilian to pass through. The position of the VRS, however, was no, the civilians can pass but not the military men. Can you confirm that? Am I right or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence as tendered reflects the fact that the Muslim position was that they wanted the entire column out, and the fact that Colonel Pandurevic had indicated that his position was the civilians could go out but that the military would remain in the custody of the VRS. And because of the circumstances that followed, what ended up happening, as reflected by Colonel Pandurevic, was that the compromise, whether it was planned or not, the compromise solution that he reported was that, "I couldn't control it either way, but at least I can say that those Muslim military who went out went out unarmed." So the two positions are reflected and then the end result being as Colonel Pandurevic discusses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we conclude that when Pandurevic says, "Let them go," he's referring to the whole column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this regard and because I read this in conjunction with the above paragraph, I would say no, only because I do not believe that at this point in time, in time sequence, that the enormity of the situation that is reflected in the 16 July 1995 interim combat report has occurred on the 15th of July. On the 15th of July, in the morning, we have the Muslim side trying to initiate contact. There is no reflection that contact is returned or that any discussions are made during the day of the 15th. So because of that and because of the way I read this, I wouldn't come to the conclusion that if no one takes responsibility, I will be forced to let them go. I would not take that comment as relating to the column at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we now go into closed session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that Judge Fouad Riad can put his questions, bearing in mind that it is now 2.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it all right? [In English] I just want a clarification about some of your answers to my colleagues. You mentioned concerning the replacement by General Krstic to General Zivanovic, that perhaps Zivanovic was not in agreement with the plan or with Mladic's attitude in that operation. And I think that was an answer to Judge Rodrigues, and you said this was one of the two or three theories that you held. Previously I asked you about that and you didn't give me your theories, so what are the other one or two theories?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first theory is as you've stated, that he did not agree with the operation and chose to depart. The second theory is that because of preexisting health conditions, that that was a planned move between operation Krivaja-95 as planned and operation Stupcanica-95 as planned, and in fact that was a manifestation of what did occur. So again, I can't prove either of those two theories. The third theory, and again, entering the realm of speculation, is the fact that we know from our information that certainly by late July 1995, the relationship between President Karadzic as a civilian head of the government and General Mladic was extremely rocky, reflected by the fact that on 4 August he tried to fire General Mladic or at least remove him from his position as the Commander of the Main Staff. Knowing that General Zivanovic was in fact -- had a long association with General Mladic, as I outlined to Judge Rodrigues, the theory offers itself up that President Karadzic may have removed, on his own volition, General Zivanovic as a check in the growing balance of power between him and General Mladic. And again, in this case, those are three theories, and I'm not in a position with evidence to support either one of those theories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the events could not put more weight on one of the theories?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be probably unfair for me to infer that General Zivanovic after the fact should have been expected to publicly stand up and decry what happened if he disagreed with it. He lives in Serbia, as our last knowledge of him is. Those are still his people, and at a point in time particularly in 1995, late 1995, when the Serbian people and the army of the Republika Srpska is under attack from the Croatians, from the Bosnian-Muslims, and from NATO in that regard, and maintaining unity at all costs would be a plausible goal, in that regard it would be unfair for me to expect General Zivanovic to stand up at that time and say things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The other answer you gave, also to Judge Rodrigues I think, was the following: I think you said that a lot of the action of the Drina Corps were reactive acts. You used the word "reactive," which means that they were not planned. I just put this together with one of your statements, a very clear one. It was on the 30th of June, you said that, "The individual pieces infer that there was a plan or a knowledge of a plan by the individuals who were part of the process." And you mentioned the guarding of the prisoners, the arrangement of the transportation, and the execution system. So do you think all this was reactive now in -- put it now in perspective? How do you reconcile this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, it's a long-term and a short-term argument. Within the scope of the short-term problem of trying to assemble the buses, it was reactive. There did not appear to be a plan several days out that they would need these buses. Now, again, somebody put together a plan rapidly and did that, but it doesn't -- again, it doesn't -- to me, looking at the material, it doesn't infer that somebody thought this out more than two days in advance. The same way with the identification of sites in Bratunac for Muslim males and sites in Zvornik for Muslim males, again, reactive in a sense of the planning didn't look to occur long term. They weren't looking three or four days out, which is what one would expect from a corps staff, that they're looking four, five, six days in the future, reactive insomuch as we have a situation that is occurring now or will be occurring within a very rapid period of time, and we have to do something immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that apply to the executions of such a big, a big number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If going back to when the first series of executions occurred that could infer being planned, and in this case we'll use the Cerska Valley executions of the early afternoon of 13 July, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That was planned in advance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inference that I make is that somewhere between that and the period of 11 and 12 July, the plan must have been hatched. Again, in my mind, that reflects short-term planning. It does not reflect a long-term plan of execution. Not execution in a criminal sense in this one, just one how executes a plan. I wouldn't take the events that are occurring on the 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th of July and beyond and take that back, and to say that on 2 July 1995 or 4 July 1995, when Krivaja-1995, the plan, was hatched, that that was in any way part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Putting this in perspective with an answer you gave to Judge Wald, you expressed some kind of a transition mark. You said that there was some kind -- the fact that they had something like 10.000 Muslims in prison was a leverage to the BiH and to the international community, and it seemed rather strange that they would not use this leverage and apparently execute the people, and you wondered if they had a higher plan in that sort. What could be the higher plan which would override the leverage, this very strong leverage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that regard, what I was noting was that one would believe that rather than executing the Muslim men, that if they were to come into possession of them and hold them in Potocari, that within the political spectrum, that would give them an enormous bargaining chip or political leverage over the situation. And again in answer to Judge Wald's question, and there I entered the realm of speculation knowingly, one has to wonder why something like that was not accomplished, and the manifestations of the executions as we saw them took place. There had to have been some trigger to do that, one would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You say "trigger" or "higher purpose" or "plan."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I use the phrase "trigger," I use some event or some decision that had to have been made by somebody somewhere that, "No. We're not going to hold these individuals as prisoners. We're going to in fact continue or begin a long series of process of executions." So somewhere apparently somebody made a conscientious decision one way or another which way it was going to be, and I don't have the evidence base and I don't have, as a result of my reading it, I can't put my finger on when, where, and under what circumstances that individual decision was made. The best that I can do is offer the windows of when this could have occurred, to the Court, based on the known facts that I have in my possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So just to finish. I'm closing down. Could you consider this was reactive or as a strategy, a policy of a higher status, owing to the number of executions and, as you said, the coordination and so on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly this operation as we saw it, reflected the plans, policies, and intent of the army of Republika Srpska with General Mladic as its head and the Drina Corps as the major component in East Bosnia that was accomplishing that. I cannot take it to the next step and say that that intent and that directive was at the guidance of President Karadzic based on the military documents and information that I've evaluated. So I can't make that link with the material that I have available to me. The inference is that the army could not have gotten away with doing this, one, without certainly the knowledge of the president of the republic, who had his own independent intelligence and security-gathering apparatus. And we know from the 18 July 1995 report from Captain First Class Momir Nikolic, that certainly that apparatus was present there in one regard, because they gave an opinion to Captain Nikolic as to what they believed the status of multi-national workers and more importantly the status of Muslims who were working for the UN and for MSF were under that regard. So clearly, President Karadzic had his intelligence collection information and assets out there and was listening. Certainly the Minister of the Interior and his forces were throughout that whole area. So again, I can't say that President Karadzic knew while it was occurring, but I can say that all of the tools and all of the mechanisms which the president of the republic should have had to keep him informed were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In normal conditions, having come to almost 3.00, we've worked very hard, and I apologise to the interpreters, because we had two breaks and one that was a shorter one, but I think that the interpreters can understand the work we are doing here, and they are also a part of the working team, and we have a spirit of solidarity amongst us. I risk being accused and even being criticised, but I'm saying this to try and make up for this. I think now that we have some documents to tender, and I would like to ask whether we can tender the documents without the presence of the witness. Then we can do it on Monday, or maybe the witness can come just for that purpose. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm prepared to defer until Monday the regulation of these documents. I intend to meet with counsel after today's session. We perhaps can present to the Court a more expedited presentation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you need the presence -- maybe I should ask Mr. McCloskey, but it's more or less the same thing. Do you need the witness for the tendering of documents, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe we need his presence, but he's still working on various investigations. So he's close by if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a Defence document to be tendered, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it's document D24, and that's General Krstic's waiver to be presented today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that there was no objection on the part of the Prosecution, so that the Defence Exhibit is admitted into evidence. So I think we really have come to the end of our work. All of us have supported a great deal, a great deal of strain, as well as the witness, and we do thank Mr. Butler very warmly for his understanding. You have produced a great deal of information to us, the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Judges, and we thank you very much. I apologise once again to everyone, but I wholeheartedly wish you a well-deserved, good weekend. These things do happen on Fridays, so you will an opportunity to recover. So, Mr. Butler, thank you once again for coming, and have a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of July, 2000, at 9.30 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.55 p.m.,
